01 / Internship project

Rokid AR Guide

An exhibition guide for Rokid smart glasses, built during my internship at Aspire Digital Technology. A visitor looks at an exhibit, hears a reviewed introduction, and can then ask questions about it.

OverviewEngineeringResults & evidence
Role
Project team lead
When
Jul–Aug 2026
Stack
Android, MediaCodec, Python
Hardware
Rokid RV101, NanoPC T6

What I did

  • Led the project team and integrated the Android camera pipeline with the Python recognition service.
  • Prioritized recent frames and helped keep exhibit context, reviewed introductions and generated follow-up answers separate.
  • Email me about this project

The situation

A visitor walks through an exhibition wearing the glasses. The guide has to work out which exhibit is in front of them, give a short introduction, and answer questions without drifting to a different exhibit. Text and speech have to stay short enough to follow while standing in front of the object.

From glasses to recognition

The RV101 glasses stream video over Rokid's CXR-M link to an Android app running on a NanoPC T6 board. The Android side decodes the stream with MediaCodec, picks a recent frame instead of working through a backlog, and sends it to the Python backend as a multipart image request. Recognition happens in the backend.

I worked on this Android-to-Python integration. Choosing newer frames keeps recognition tied to what the visitor is looking at now, not to where they were looking a moment ago.

Keeping the exhibit as context

Once an exhibit is recognized, it becomes the context for the conversation. Answers use reviewed knowledge about that exhibit. A late response to the previous exhibit is a real failure mode when the visitor turns away: the guide clears stale display content and uses context generation tokens to discard the old answer when it arrives. Newer decoded frames take priority for the same reason.

Reviewed introductions and generated answers

The system handles two kinds of content separately. Each exhibit's introduction comes from reviewed material. Follow-up questions get generated answers, grounded in that exhibit's reviewed knowledge. The separation is in how the system stores and routes content.

I also adjusted how text and speech are presented on the glasses so visitors could follow them.

Debugging a connection that stopped halfway

Bluetooth initialization succeeded, but the Socket connection never started. I traced the connection state and asynchronous callbacks: a state flag was blocking the next stage before the callback could advance it. I revised the state transitions, callback handling and exception paths rather than treating Bluetooth success as a completed connection.

The sampling rate was raised from approximately one to two frames per second while retaining one request in flight, latest-frame selection and consecutive-frame confirmation. This bounds the queue without claiming measured end-to-end latency.

A separate dialogue phase

After the recognition and introduction flow was accepted, we froze that baseline and developed free dialogue separately. The guide finishes the reviewed introduction before opening the listening phase, so a question does not interrupt the exhibit presentation.

The backend's TourSession retains the current and previous exhibit. References such as “this one” and comparisons are resolved against that session before reviewed evidence is sent to Dify. The model service is not the source of truth for exhibit state.

When evidence is insufficient, the answer explains the gap and suggests two answerable questions about the current exhibit. A scene guard prevents competing glasses features from interfering with the guide's microphone and display.

Keeping service failures out of the subtitles

A temporary SSL failure in the model service triggered the reviewed-knowledge fallback, but an early implementation appended internal service-status text to the visitor's subtitles. I separated operational status from presentation: logs retain the failure and fallback route, while HUD text contains only the reviewed answer.

This fix addresses error presentation. It is not evidence that the service never fails or that fallback answers cover every visitor question.

Recognition path

Result and status

Three August 4 device demo rounds passed: one reference-image diagnostic and two physical exhibit flows with recognition, grounded answers, visible HUD text and audible speech. The August 19 handoff still listed six on-site checks for manual confirmation. Scope and limits

What was tested on hardware

August 4 records three demonstration rounds on RV101 glasses with a NanoPC T6. The first used reference images; the next two used physical exhibits and confirmed the recognition-to-answer-to-HUD/TTS chain. Software regression checks cover additional guide behavior, while final on-site acceptance remained a separate step.

Software handoff, August 19
Regression
348 Python tests passed in the final handoff record.
Dialogue
181 / 181 evaluation cases passed; this is suite coverage, not visitor answer-quality accuracy.
Knowledge
7 knowledge objects, 36 published chunks and 11 sources; retrieval checks passed 45 / 45 cases.
Device release
Android unit checks, lint and APK build passed. Final glasses end-to-end acceptance still required manual field checks.

These are dated software gates. They do not replace the earlier hardware demos or prove that every exhibit was tested on site.

What remains to check

That coverage is narrower than it might sound:

  • Seven knowledge objects were published to the guide. That counts content. It does not mean seven exhibits passed on site.
  • The final handoff record on August 19 still listed six items waiting for manual confirmation on site.
  • Nothing here measures recognition accuracy, latency, answer quality, or behaviour on other Rokid hardware.
